c018.front: How do NVL, NVL2, COALESCE and NULLIF differ?
c018.back: NVL(a,b): b when a is NULL. NVL2(a,x,y): x when a is NOT NULL, otherwise y. COALESCE: the first value that is not NULL; the arguments must be of the same type family, and evaluation stops at the first one found. NULLIF(a,b): NULL when a=b, otherwise a.
c018.try_sql:
-- Predict each column: NVL, NVL2, COALESCE, NULLIF
SELECT NVL(NULL, 'b') AS nvl_r,
       NVL2(1, 'x', 'y') AS nvl2_r,
       COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'c') AS coalesce_r,
       NULLIF(5, 5) AS nullif_r
FROM   dual;

c019.front: How do DECODE and CASE treat NULL?
c019.back: DECODE considers NULL and NULL equal, so they match. A simple CASE compares with =, so WHEN NULL never matches. Use CASE WHEN x IS NULL.
c019.try_sql:
-- Employee 108 has no department: DECODE matches the NULL, a simple CASE does not
SELECT e.employee_id,
       DECODE(e.department_id, NULL, 'brak', 'jest') AS by_decode,
       CASE e.department_id WHEN NULL THEN 'brak' ELSE 'jest' END AS by_case,
       CASE WHEN e.department_id IS NULL THEN 'brak' ELSE 'jest' END AS by_is_null
FROM   employees e
WHERE  e.employee_id IN (107, 108);

c020.front: What does fm do in a format?
c020.back: Fill mode: it removes leading zeros and padding spaces (for example with names from Month and Day). It works as a toggle: a second fm turns it off again.
c020.try_sql:
-- Compare the brackets: without fm, with fm, and with fm a second time (turns it off)
SELECT '[' || TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'DD Month YYYY') || ']' AS bez_fm,
       '[' || TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'fmDD Month YYYY') || ']' AS z_fm,
       '[' || TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'fmDD fmMonth YYYY') || ']' AS fm_dwa_razy
FROM   dual;

c021.back: ####### (7 characters, no error): the mask is too small for the number. A number mask also has one leading place for the sign, so the width is the mask length plus one.
c021.try_sql:
-- The mask is too narrow: only # instead of an error
SELECT TO_CHAR(1234.5, '999.99') AS za_mala,
       TO_CHAR(1234.5, '9999.99') AS pasuje
FROM   dual;

c022.front: Why is it better to avoid WHERE d > '31/03/2024'?
c022.back: Because the string is converted to a date with the session's NLS_DATE_FORMAT. Another session may have a different format, and you get an error. Use DATE '2024-03-31' or TO_DATE('31/03/2024', 'DD/MM/YYYY').

c023.front: Does case matter in a format?
c023.back: Yes. The case of the element sets the case of the result: MONTH → MARCH, Month → March, month → march. The th suffix: DDth → 05TH. sp spells the number out: DDSP → FIVE.
c023.try_sql:
-- Case of the element = case of the result; th and sp
SELECT TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'MONTH') AS up,
       TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'Month') AS cap,
       TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'month') AS low,
       TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'DDth') AS th,
       TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-03-05', 'DDSP') AS sp
FROM   dual;

c024.front: How does RR differ from YY in a year format?
c024.back: For a 2-digit year, RR picks the century depending on the current year (the 00–49 and 50–99 rule). YY always takes the current century.
c024.try_sql:
-- Year '99': RR picks the previous century, YY takes the current one
SELECT TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('99', 'RR'), 'YYYY') AS rr,
       TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('99', 'YY'), 'YYYY') AS yy
FROM   dual;

c210.front: In what order are nested functions evaluated, and how deep can they be nested?
c210.back: From the inside out: each function gets the result of the function inside it. Single-row functions can be nested to any depth, group functions only to two levels.

c211.front: How do you show 'No manager' when the NUMBER column manager_id is NULL?
c211.back: NVL(TO_CHAR(e.manager_id), 'No manager'). The inner TO_CHAR makes both arguments text. NVL(e.manager_id, 'No manager') raises ORA-01722.
c211.try_sql:
-- The first query works (TO_CHAR inside), the second raises an error
SELECT e.employee_id, NVL(TO_CHAR(e.manager_id), 'No manager') AS manager
FROM   employees e
WHERE  e.employee_id IN (100, 101);
SELECT NVL(e.manager_id, 'No manager') AS manager
FROM   employees e
WHERE  e.employee_id = 100;

c212.front: A VARCHAR2 column compared with a number: which side is converted?
c212.back: The text side is converted to NUMBER: WHERE email = 100 converts every email and raises ORA-01722 when it hits text that is not a number. The operator decides the direction: '10' + 5 = 15, '10' || 5 = '105'.

c213.back: '1,234.5' and '1,234.50'. In number masks, fm removes the sign space and the trailing zeros in 9 positions. 0 positions are always printed.
c213.try_sql:
-- fm with 9 cuts the trailing zero, 0 is always printed
SELECT TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'fm9,999.99') AS z_9,
       TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'fm9,999.00') AS z_0
FROM   dual;

c214.front: DECODE without a default value, and result types in CASE?
c214.back: DECODE returns NULL when nothing matches and there is no default. The result type of DECODE comes from the first result. All results of a CASE must be of the same type family, otherwise ORA-00932.

c215.front: When does TO_DATE reject a string?
c215.back: When the date does not exist (TO_DATE('2024-02-30', 'YYYY-MM-DD'): ORA-01839) and, with the fx modifier, when the string does not match exactly ('2024-3-5' with fxYYYY-MM-DD). Without fx it accepts other separators and missing leading zeros.

c1250.front: COALESCE(1, 1/0) vs NVL(1, 1/0): what comes out?
c1250.back: 1, and error ORA-01476. COALESCE stops at the first argument that is not NULL and evaluates no further. NVL always evaluates both arguments.

c1251.back: ORA-01722 for rows outside department 10. The result type of DECODE is the type of the first result (NUMBER), so 'n/a' must become a number, and it cannot. A CASE with different types raises ORA-00932 instead.

c1252.back: 2024-03-02, and ORA-01722. With +, text is converted to NUMBER, never to DATE.

c1253.front: Do e.salary LIKE '6%' and e.hire_date LIKE '%-01-%' work (salary NUMBER, hire_date DATE)?
c1253.back: Both work, because Oracle converts the value to text itself: the number becomes '6000', and the date is written with NLS_DATE_FORMAT. That is why the second result depends on the session settings.

c1254.front: What does WHERE e.employee_id IN ('100', 'abc') give?
c1254.back: ORA-01722: every value in the list is converted to NUMBER, and 'abc' cannot be. Oracle does not skip bad values.
c1254.try_sql:
-- 'abc' cannot be converted to NUMBER: an error for the whole query
SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees e WHERE e.employee_id IN ('100', 'abc');

c1255.front: What do the number format elements MI, PR, S, L, C, G, D mean?
c1255.back: MI: a trailing minus (1,234.50-). PR: negative numbers in angle brackets <1,234.50>. S: a + or - sign. L: the local currency (NLS_CURRENCY), C: the ISO code (USD). G/D: the group and decimal separators from NLS; do not mix them with , and . (ORA-01481).
c1255.try_sql:
-- Predict each result; at the end, mixing G with . raises an error
SELECT TO_CHAR(-1234.5, '9,999.00MI') AS mi,
       TO_CHAR(-1234.5, '9,999.00PR') AS pr,
       TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'S9,999.00') AS s,
       TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'fmL9,999.00') AS l,
       TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'fmC9,999.00') AS c,
       TO_CHAR(1234.5, '9G999D00') AS gd
FROM   dual;
SELECT TO_CHAR(1234.5, '9G999.00') AS mix FROM dual;

c1256.back: '          $1,234.50' (L pads with spaces to a fixed width) and '$1,234.50'. fm removes those spaces.
c1256.try_sql:
-- L pads with spaces to a fixed width, fm removes them
SELECT '[' || TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'L9,999.00') || ']' AS l,
       '[' || TO_CHAR(1234.5, 'fmL9,999.00') || ']' AS fm_l
FROM   dual;

c1257.back: The 1st day of the CURRENT month in 2024, at midnight. Missing elements get default values: the current year and month, day 1 and time 00:00:00.
c1257.try_sql:
-- Missing elements: the current month, day 1, midnight
SELECT TO_DATE('2024', 'YYYY') AS d, SYSDATE AS teraz FROM dual;

c1258.front: RR for 49, 50 and a four-digit year (current year 2000-2049)?
c1258.back: '49' -> 2049, '50' -> 1950, '1950' stays 1950. YY always takes the current century: '99' -> 2099.
c1258.try_sql:
-- RR: 49 -> 20xx, 50 -> 19xx, 4 digits unchanged; YY: the current century
SELECT TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('49', 'RR'), 'YYYY') AS rr49,
       TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('50', 'RR'), 'YYYY') AS rr50,
       TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('1950', 'RR'), 'YYYY') AS rr1950,
       TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('99', 'YY'), 'YYYY') AS yy99
FROM   dual;

c1259.back: ORA-01830: the format ends before the whole string is read. The other way round is fine: a format longer than the string (with HH24:MI) works and gives midnight.

c1260.back: '%'. Joining with || skips NULL, so NVL never gets a NULL. Test the column itself: NVL2(col, TO_CHAR(col) || '%', 'none').
c1260.try_sql:
-- || skips NULL, so NVL never sees NULL; NVL2 tests the column itself
SELECT e.employee_id,
       NVL(TO_CHAR(e.commission_pct) || '%', 'none') AS zle,
       NVL2(e.commission_pct, TO_CHAR(e.commission_pct) || '%', 'none') AS dobrze
FROM   employees e
WHERE  e.employee_id IN (100, 101);

c1261.front: LENGTH(TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-05-05', 'Month')) vs the same with fmMonth?
c1261.back: 9 and 3. Month is padded with spaces to 9 characters (September), and fm removes those spaces. The inner function is evaluated first, then LENGTH.
c1261.try_sql:
-- Month has 9 characters with spaces, fmMonth only 3
SELECT LENGTH(TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-05-05', 'Month')) AS month_len,
       LENGTH(TO_CHAR(DATE '2024-05-05', 'fmMonth')) AS fm_len
FROM   dual;
